FOR CLAT 2027
7

BrahMos Missile Deal


• On 30 May 2026, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed
  at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore that India has signed a
  deal to supply BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles to Vietnam.

• A similar agreement with Indonesia is in its final stages,
  signalling a significant expansion of India's defence footprint in
  Southeast Asia.

• Singh said the Vietnam deal has already been concluded, though it
  has not been publicly announced yet.

BrahMos Missile Deal


What is the BrahMos Missile?

• BrahMos is a supersonic cruise missile jointly developed by India
  and Russia, named after the Brahmaputra and Moskva rivers.

• It is the world’s fastest operational supersonic cruise missile, capable
  of travelling at nearly Mach 3 (about 3 times the speed of
  sound) .

• The missile can be launched from land, sea and air platforms and
  is designed for precision strikes against both land and naval targets.

BrahMos Missile Deal



• BrahMos has a maximum range of up to 290-800 km and can carry
  warheads weighing up to 200 kg .

• It is a two-stage missile with a solid propellant booster and a liquid
  propellant ramjet system.

• The missile is based on “fire and forget” technology and uses an
  advanced guidance system for high accuracy.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• BrahMos Aerospace Private Limited (BAPL) was established
  in 1998 as a joint venture between India’s Defence Research
  and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Russia’s NPO
  Mashinostroyenia.

• India holds 50.5% of the shares, while Russia holds 49.5% of the
  shares.

• The joint venture is responsible for the design, development,
  production and marketing of the BrahMos missile system.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• Both countries maintain equal stakes in the missile’s intellectual
  property and export rights under the joint venture agreement.

• As a jointly owned technology, any proposed sale of BrahMos
  missiles to a third nation requires prior consent from both
  India and Russia.

• This dual-approval arrangement ensures that neither side can
  independently authorise exports or modify the missile configuration
  without the other’s concurrence.

BrahMos Missile Deal



• BrahMos has been adapted for multiple platforms, including
  land-based coastal defence batteries, ship-launched anti-ship
  variants, air-launched versions and submarine-launched
  configurations.

• The air-launched variant is integrated with India’s Su-30MKI
  fighter aircraft.

• The BrahMos missile is included in the fleet of the Indian Army,
  Navy and Air Force.

BrahMos Missile Deal



• India and Russia are jointly developing BrahMos-2 , a hypersonic
  cruise missile inspired by Russia’s 3M22 Zircon missile.

• BrahMos-2 is designed to travel at Mach 6 to Mach 8 (6 to 8 times
  the speed of sound) with a range of up to 1,500 km .

• The missile will use a scramjet engine, and DRDO successfully
  tested a scramjet combustor in April 2025.

BrahMos Missile Deal



• The Philippines became the first overseas customer for BrahMos,
  signing a contract worth nearly $375 million in January 2022.

• The deal covered shore-based anti-ship missile systems, training and
  logistics support.

• The Philippines received the first batch of BrahMos missiles in 2024 ,
  with a second batch delivered in April 2025.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• India’s defence exports have grown nearly tenfold in the space of
  five years, reaching a record high of about $2.76 billion in 2024-
  25 .

• The BrahMos deals with Vietnam and Indonesia alone would add well
  over $1 billion to that figure.

• India has set an ambitious target of achieving ₹50,000 crore in
  defence exports by 2030 .

BrahMos Missile Deal


• Exporters are required to procure an export license from the
  Chief Controller of Explosives under the regulatory framework
  governing export of munitions.

• The Ministry of Defence has amended guidelines to simplify the
  export authorisation process for both private and public sector units.

• The BrahMos missile, being a strategically significant weapon system,
  is considered for export only to select friendly partners.

BrahMos Missile Deal

Shangri La Dialogue –

• It also known as the Asia Security Summit and is an annual
  defence and security forum held in Singapore, hosted by the
  London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies
  (IISS).

• It is regarded as Asia’s most important defence summit, where
  defence ministers, military chiefs, and security experts from across
  the globe gather to discuss pressing regional security challenges.

• The forum serves as a crucial platform for dialogue, confidence-
  building, and "defence diplomacy" in the Asia-Pacific region.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• The Shangri-La Dialogue was first held in 2002 at the Shangri-La
  Hotel in Singapore, from which it derives its name.

• It was established to fill a significant gap: the lack of a regular,
  high-level multilateral security forum in the Asia-Pacific region.

• The forum has grown substantially from its first conference, which
  attracted delegates from around 20 countries, to becoming a premier
  annual global security event.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• The 23rd Shangri-La Dialogue in 2026 saw representatives
  from 44 countries in attendance, including 54 ministerial-level
  delegates and over 42 Chiefs of Defence Forces.

• High-profile participants included the US Secretary of defense,
  Japan's Defence Minister, and Vietnam's President who
  delivered the keynote address.

• China's defence minister has missed the forum for the second
  consecutive year, sending a delegation of experts and scholars led
  by a PLA National Defence University professor.

BrahMos Missile Deal


MTCR –

• Missile Technology Control Regime was established in 1987
  by G7 nations to prevent the proliferation of missiles capable of
  delivering weapons of mass destruction (WMD).

• Operates through informal political understanding among 35
  member states, providing voluntary export guidelines to control the
  spread of missile technology.

• India officially joined the MTCR in 2016, becoming a full member.

BrahMos Missile Deal


DRDO –

• Defence Research and Development Organisation was
  founded in 1958 by merging the Technical Development
  Establishments (TDEs) with the Defence Science Organisation (DSO).

• Headquartered at DRDO Bhawan, Rajaji Marg, New Delhi.

• Motto: “Balasya Mulam Vigyanam” (The source of strength is
  science). Operates a network of 41 laboratories and 5 Young
  Scientist Laboratories (DYSLs).

Recent News –

• India and Vietnam officially signed the Enhanced Comprehensive
  Strategic Partnership (ECSP) agreement on 6 May
  2026 during the visit of Vietnamese President To Lam to India.

• This was accompanied by the signing of 13 documents. The
  landmark agreement builds on the 2007 Strategic Partnership and the
  2016 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

• The upgrade was marked by the signing of $135 million in
  defence credit lines, including pacts for digital payment
  cooperation and rare earth minerals.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• The Vietnam agreement is valued at approximately ₹5,800 crore
  (about $629 million), ranking among Hanoi's largest defence
  acquisitions in recent memory.

• The package includes shore-based coastal defence missile batteries,
  an initial batch of missiles, training and long-term logistical support.

• Reports suggest that Vietnam may later acquire the air-launched
  version of the missile as well.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• India and Vietnam have agreed to establish a “2+2” ministerial
  dialogue , bringing together foreign and defence ministers.

• India has instituted this format with only a select group of strategic
  partners, including the United States, Japan, Australia and
  Russia.

• The dialogue will further deepen bilateral strategic and security
  cooperation between the two nations.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• Both sides have agreed to enhance defence systems
  procurement between the two countries, indicating potential Indian
  military exports to Vietnam in the years ahead.

• Vietnam is also studying India’s proposal for MRO (Maintenance,
  Repair and Overhaul) support for its Russian-origin Su-30 fighter
  aircraft and Kilo-class submarines.

• The ECSP prioritises core-technology domains and provides expertise
  to manufacture high-tech defence equipment.

BrahMos Missile Deal


• Vietnam is a critical pillar of India’s Act East Policy and a key
  strategic partner in the Indo-Pacific region.

• Vietnam has also joined the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative
  (IPOI), a maritime cooperation framework launched by India in
  2019.

• Both nations share deep concerns over maritime security and
  freedom of navigation in the South China Sea.

BSF


• On 26 May 2026, Union Home Minister Amit Shah directed
  authorities to enforce a “zero tolerance” policy towards illegal
  constructions within 15 kilometres of the international border and
  demolish all such structures.

• Shah was speaking at a security review meeting near the
  international border in Rajasthan’s Bikaner, where he assessed
  security-related issues concerning the border.

• He emphasised that the Border Security Force (BSF) must
  strengthen its preparedness against illegal smuggling, infiltration, and
  cross-border activities.

BSF


What is the Border Security Force (BSF)?

• The BSF is India’s primary border guarding force, raised after the
  enactment of the Border Security Force Act in September 1968.

• It is a paramilitary force under the administrative control of
  the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

• The BSF is responsible for securing India’s land borders during
  peacetime and preventing trans-border crimes.

BSF


• Before 1965, border security was largely the responsibility of state
  police, but the Indo-Pak war of 1965 exposed gaps in border
  management.

• The BSF was created to provide a dedicated, centrally-controlled
  force to guard India’s international borders.

• As a BSF officer later explained, border areas were sparsely
  populated with few police stations, making a specialised border force
  necessary.

BSF


• The Border Security Force Act, 1968 provides for the constitution
  and regulation of an “Armed Force of the Union” for ensuring the
  security of the borders of India.

• Section 139 of the Act empowers the central government, by
  notification, to designate areas adjoining the border where the BSF
  can exercise powers to prevent offences under specified laws.

• The Act also establishes a separate Security Force Court to try
  members of the BSF for offences under the Act.

BSF


• Guarding India’s international borders during peacetime and
  preventing illegal infiltration, smuggling and cross-border
  crimes.

• Creating a sense of security among people living in border areas.

• Assisting state police and other agencies in maintaining law and
  order when required.

BSF


• The BSF is empowered to arrest, search and seize under several
  central laws, including the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC),
  1973, the Passports Act, 1967, and the Passport (Entry into
  India) Act, 1920.

• The BSF also exercises powers under the Narcotic Drugs and
  Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 and other
  anti-smuggling laws.

• However, the BSF has no power to investigate or prosecute; it
  must hand over arrested persons and seized goods to the state police
  within 24 hours.

BSF


• Before the October 2021 notification, the BSF could exercise its
  powers within 15 km of the border in Punjab, West Bengal and
  Assam.

• In the northeastern states of Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura,
  Nagaland and Meghalaya, the BSF had jurisdiction over
  the entire state.

• In the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, the
  BSF also had jurisdiction over the entire UT.

BSF


Other Forces –

• The Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) are central
  paramilitary forces under the administrative control of the
  Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

• They are deployed for internal security, border guarding,
  counter-insurgency and other specialised tasks.

• The five main CAPFs are the BSF, CRPF, ITBP, SSB and CISF; the
  Assam Rifles is also often included under the CAPF umbrella.

BSF


• The Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) is India’s largest
  central armed police force, with a sanctioned strength of over 11
  lakh personnel.

• It is the primary force for internal security, counter-insurgency and
  law and order duties, and is not a border guarding force.

• It was originally raised as the Crown Representative's Police on
  27 July 1939; often deployed in areas affected by left-wing
  extremism (Naxalism) and in Jammu & Kashmir.

BSF


• The Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) was raised immediately
  after the 1962 Indo-China war to guard India’s northern borders
  with China.

• It is the only police force with specialised expertise in high-altitude
  mountain warfare, guarding the 2,115-km border from Karakoram
  Pass to Lipulekh.

• The ITBP also undertakes disaster management duties and has been
  deployed for internal security tasks.

BSF


• The Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) is the border guarding force for
  India’s borders with Nepal and Bhutan.

• It was originally raised as the Special Service Bureau in 1963 and
  was renamed the Sashastra Seema Bal in 2004.

• The SSB has equipped itself with state-of-the-art surveillance
  equipment, including UAVs and automatic face/number-plate
  recognition systems.

BSF


• The Assam Rifles was raised in 1835 as the Cachar Levy to protect
  British tea estates and settlements.

• It is the oldest paramilitary force in India and has served in two
  World Wars and the 1962 Sino-Indian war.

• The Assam Rifles has a dual control structure: administrative
  control is with the MHA, but operational control is with the Indian
  Army, which is under the Ministry of Defence.

BSF



• The Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) is responsible for
  providing security to major public sector undertakings, airports,
  seaports, and other critical infrastructure.

• It is not a border guarding force but plays a crucial role in
  protecting India’s economic and industrial assets.

• The CISF is also deployed for disaster management and has its own
  fire service wing.

BSF



• On 11 October 2021, the Centre issued a notification extending the
  BSF’s jurisdiction to 50 km from the international border in Punjab,
  West Bengal and Assam.

• In Gujarat, the BSF’s jurisdiction was reduced from 80 km to 50
  km to align with other states.

• Rajasthan’s limit was kept unchanged at 50 km, while the
  northeastern states continued to be covered under full-state
  jurisdiction.

BSF


• Within the larger 50-km zone, the BSF can exercise powers only
  under three laws: the CrPC, the Passport (Entry into India)
  Act, 1920, and the Passports Act, 1967.

• For all other central legislation (including the NDPS Act and
  Customs Act), the 15-km limit remains in force.

• Research Fellow Pushpita Das of the MP-IDSA noted that the
  expansion emphasises prevention of illegal migration and
  cross-border crimes, not investigation or prosecution.

BSF


• The government cited the increased use of drones and UAVs for
  smuggling arms, drugs and fake currency across the border.

• Cattle smuggling and the need to tackle “radical groups” trying to
  destabilise Punjab were also reasons.

• The Centre argued that smugglers often took refuge outside the
  earlier 15-km jurisdiction, making a larger operational zone
  necessary.

BSF


• The Punjab government moved the Supreme Court in 2021
  challenging the expansion, arguing that it encroached upon
  the constitutional jurisdiction of the state over police and law
  and order.

• The West Bengal government also strongly objected, accusing the
  Centre of undermining federalism and the powers of the state police.

• The state governments argued that “police” and “public order”
  are State subjects under the Seventh Schedule of the
  Constitution, and the Centre had no authority to unilaterally expand
  the BSF’s powers.

BSF


• The Punjab government’s challenge is pending before the Supreme
  Court, which has framed key questions, including whether the
  50-km extension impairs the functions of the state police.

• The Court is examining whether the concurrent
  jurisdiction conferred on the BSF, with primacy to the BSF,
  violates the federal scheme.

• The case also raises questions about the constitutional validity of
  the 2021 notification and the extent of the Centre’s power under
  Section 139 of the BSF Act.

BSF


• Under the Seventh Schedule, “police” and “public order” fall
  under Entry 2 of the State List, meaning states have exclusive
  legislative and executive power over policing.

• The Centre’s power to deploy central forces is derived from Entry 2A
  of the Concurrent List (“Criminal law”) and Entry 1 of the Union
  List (“Defence of India”).

• The legal question is whether border security is an aspect of
  “defence” (Union List) or “police” (State List).
